items.title: Thrown in with Giggs and Beckham: how Manchester United tried to get Billy Kenny
items.author: Billy Kenny
items.content:
Former Everton midfielder, known as the ‘Goodison Gazza’, recalls being made to feel special by Alex Ferguson in this autobiography extract

“So this is the scouser ya been goin’ on aboot then …” My face turned Manchester United red. Scanning the room full of smiles and staring eyes, I identified the mystery Scottish voice as the man who’d just become the first player to score more than 20 league goals for the club since George Best in the 1960s. “Good answer,” replied Brian McClair after following up on my smile and nod by asking whether I supported Everton or Liverpool. “Ye’ll dee well ’ere laddie.”

Brian Kidd had just introduced me to the Man United first team by silencing the room to draw attention to my presence. “Lads, this is Billy from up the road,” he said. I was still starstruck from seeing all these famous faces as my chauffeur for the day, Eric Harrison, pulled up in the car park at The Cliff a few minutes earlier. Paul McGrath. Mark Hughes. Bryan Robson. Kevin Moran. Norman Whiteside. I ticked them all off in my head. Thank fuck I was developing an ear for everyday Glaswegian because after a bit of piss-taking from the first-teamers about being a scouser, I found myself standing in an office at the end of a short and narrow corridor, shaking hands with another one.

Continue reading...

items.lbText:
‘I wouldn’t feel comfortable … I don’t think we deserved it’

Manchester United finished second to City in 2011-12

Wayne Rooney does not believe it would be appropriate for Manchester City to be stripped of titles for breaching Premier League financial rules, even if it gave him another Premier League winner’s medal, as that would be unfair of the City players and staff whose endeavours secured success.

City are waiting to find out what sanctions they will face after being found guilty of more than a hundred charges , with an array of potential punishments on the table. Rooney was part of the United squad in 2011-12 that finished second to City on goal difference after Sergio Agüero’s last-minute winner secured the Premier League trophy for Roberto Mancini’s side on the final day.

City continue to deny any wrongdoing and are confident of overturning the verdict on appeal.

“I wouldn’t feel comfortable about accepting another Premier League medal if I’m being honest, because I don’t think we deserve it,” Rooney said on the Stick to United podcast. “We didn’t do enough ‌that season to win the league. I’m thinking as their players, they’re doing everything they can to win the Premier League title and in their minds they’ve done it. And if that happened to me, if all of a sudden Manchester ⁠United have been doing the same and I’m getting my Premier League medals taken away from me, I’d be absolutely devastated.”

Rooney would still want City punished if they are ultimately guilty of wrongdoing. “I’d put them in the lowest league they can go in and then put restrictions on them in terms of how much money they can spend for the next three or four seasons,” the former England captain said.

Javier Tebas, the La Liga president and a longtime critic of City, wants the punishment to fit the crime. “We’re trying to make football sustainable ‌and clean across all competitions,” he said at the Peak Performance + Health Summit in London. “As many ‌clubs are saying, titles were lost that shouldn’t have been lost to other clubs. What has happened is very important, and we hope it marks ‌a turning point, not just for the Premier League.

“The Manchester City case has implications across Europe. There should be a punishment that sets an example. Breaking them [the rules] for more than 10 years ... is very serious. The punishment should therefore be severe, not only to set an example, but because the rules were broken.”

items.lbText:
Manchester City have kicked off the campaign with five victories in a row but the title race is a marathon not a sprint

T he first international window gives us time to take stock and make sense of what has happened in the early weeks of the Premier League season. Manchester City are the only team to have won all five of their matches. They have started life after Pep Guardiola in the best way possible on the pitch, opening a three-point gap over champions Arsenal, but how important is a fast start?

Of course, we do not yet know the punishment they may face for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rules so, for the purposes of this article, we will put that matter to the side.

Enzo Maresca’s side became the 15th different team to win their opening five games of a Premier League season, and it’s the fourth occasion City have managed it. They have only won the title in one of the three previous seasons, though. They won the league in 2023-24, but failed to capitalise on their five early wins in 2015-16 and 2016-17.

That follows a wider trend across the league. Only four of the 14 teams that have won their first five matches of the season have gone on to win the title (29%): Manchester City in 2023-24, Liverpool in 2019-20, and Chelsea in 2009-10 and 2005-06.

Perhaps most importantly, all four teams went on to add to their winning streak to start those seasons. Chelsea in 2009-10 and Manchester City in 2023-24 extended their run by another game (six wins); Liverpool started with eight wins in 2019-20; and Chelsea (nine wins in 2005-06) went on the longest winning run to start a Premier League season.

Tottenham hold the record for the most consecutive wins to start a top-flight league season. They won their first 11 games in 1960-61 and, unsurprisingly, won the title that campaign. But a winning start does not guarantee success, as Manchester United found in 1985-86. Despite winning their first 10 games that season (and remaining unbeaten in their first 15) under Ron Atkinson, they collapsed and ended the season in fourth place.

It must be said, City have benefited from having an easy run of fixtures. According to the Opta Power Rankings , City had the second-easiest start this season, with their opponents having an average rating of 91.2. Only Liverpool (91.1) were handed a simpler start to the season by the Premier League fixture computer.

Another statistic that will give City fans reason for pause is that none of the previous seven clubs to start a Premier League season with exactly five wins have gone on to win the title in that campaign.

The most recent of those was Liverpool last season. The reigning champions won games against Bournemouth, Newcastle, Arsenal , Burnley and Everton to open the 2025-26 campaign before losing four in a row. The fact Liverpool won four of their first five games with goals scored after the 83rd minute pointed to their run being unsustainable, and so it proved.

Question marks about City’s defensive qualities this season suggest this may be another unsustainable winning run. Their credentials will be tested when the Premier League returns and they visit Anfield to face Liverpool, who are still unbeaten under new boss Andoni Iraola.

The lowest position a team has finished after winning their first five games of a season is sixth (Newcastle United in 1994-95), although that did come in a 42-game campaign. Looking back at all English top-flight history, City’s current streak is the 40th different occasion of a team winning their first five games in a season. Just 14 of the previous 39 have gone on to win the league title (36%).

The average points won by Premier League champions from the first five games across the previous 34 Premier League campaigns is 11.3, which is above the total secured by Arsenal last season. They won 10 points from their first five games, dropping points by losing at Liverpool and drawing against Manchester City at home. Mikel Arteta’s side have started this season better this time around, winning 12 points from a possible 15, with their only blemish the shock 3-0 loss at Brighton.

The fewest points eventual Premier League champions have won from their first five games was in the inaugural season in 1992-93. Manchester United won only seven points from their first five matches (two wins, one draw and two defeats), but Alex Ferguson’s side recovered and finished 10 points clear of runners up Aston Villa after the 42-game season.

No team has won a Premier League title in a 38-game season after winning fewer than eight points from their first five matches. United have won the league four times after winning exactly eight points from their opening five games (in 1998-99, 2002-03, 2007-08 and 2008-09), with City replicating that feat in 2020-21. What we’re trying to say is, Hull City and Newcastle fans, it’s still possible.

The most astonishing turnaround by title winners has to be Sunderland ’s effort in 1912-13, though. They failed to win any of their first seven games, drawing two and losing the other five, but they went on to win the First Division title. With just two points for a win back then, it was easier for teams to recover from a run of poor results; a monumental comeback nevertheless.

items.title: Every saint has a past: how man at heart of City’s first scandal became a United hero | Sean Ingle
items.author: Sean Ingle
items.content:
Billy Meredith helped win City their first major honours more than a hundred years ago, was banned by the FA – then went and repeated the trick on the red side of Manchester

When the Manchester City decision finally dropped, the Guardian’s verdict was damning. “FOOTBALL SENSATION – MANCHESTER CITY’S GRAVE OFFENCES – HEAVY PUNISHMENTS”, the headline read. “It is now proved that the club had for years systematically broken the rules of the Football Association by very unscrupulous means.”

But these words weren’t written last Friday. Instead they were penned more than 120 years ago, at the culmination of English football’s first big illicit payments scandal.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Billy Meredith helped win City their first major honours more than a hundred years ago, was banned by the FA – then went and repeated the trick on the red side of Manchester

W hen the Manchester City decision finally dropped, the Guardian’s verdict was damning. “FOOTBALL SENSATION – MANCHESTER CITY’S GRAVE OFFENCES – HEAVY PUNISHMENTS”, the headline read. “It is now proved that the club had for years systematically broken the rules of the Football Association by very unscrupulous means.”

But these words weren’t written last Friday . Instead they were penned more than 120 years ago, at the culmination of English football’s first big illicit payments scandal.

Back then City were a club rapidly on the up, with money and attitude to burn – which might sound familiar. Yet having won the FA Cup in 1904, everything began to unravel.

It started on the final day of the 1905 season, when City were on the verge of winning the title only to lose against Aston Villa in a match that involved punches and literal mud-slinging . Far more seriously, City’s star player, Billy Meredith, was also heard offering a £10 bribe to the Villa captain, Alec Leake, to throw the game.

Some say it was not serious. To this day no one knows the mysterious spectator who reported it. But it created a butterfly effect that led to Meredith being suspended for a season, and ramifications that lasted for decades.

Soon after, when Meredith was seen still hanging around City despite his ban, the FA launched a fresh investigation into the club’s finances. It found that not only was City’s gate money being funnelled into the private accounts of club directors, it was being used to give off-the-books payments to players.

Meredith, for instance, was on £6 a week when the maximum wage was £4. And he was far from the only one being given a little extra on the side. It led to the FA banning 17 players from playing for City again, while two of the club’s directors were banned for life.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme. So is what happened to City all those years ago relevant to modern times? Yes, absolutely.

First off, the 1906 case proves that strong punishments work. While City were hardly the only club to be making similar illicit payments, the FA’s sanctions led to the club slipping down the table, being relegated three years later, and not winning the title until 1937.

That City team also offered an early example of one of football’s immutable laws of gravity. The faster a club rises, the more its foundations may be shaky or unsustainable, and the more it is likely to plummet back to earth.

The other interesting thing in all this? While City had the book thrown at them , Meredith enjoyed a redemption arc that continues to this day.

It helped that some felt he had been unfairly targeted for trying to set up a players’ union and campaigning for the abolition of the maximum wage. The wiry winger could certainly play too, which certainly didn’t hurt either.

Indeed no less a judge than David Lacey, the Guardian’s legendary football correspondent, described Meredith as ranking “with that of Stanley Matthews in the history of the British game”.

And when Manchester United fans voted Eric Cantona as their greatest ever player in 2001, Lacey suggested that a couple of decades earlier they would have gone for George Best, and before that Meredith himself.

The fact that Meredith, who turned out for City from 1894 to 1905 and again from 1921 to 1924, is also in United’s hall of fame marks him out as a unique and substantial force.

Intriguingly, those switches across Manchester don’t appear to have attracted much condemnation. Indeed, when Meredith played in the Manchester derby in 1910, the Guardian’s man on the ground was left unimpressed by the lack of fire and venom.

“Both sides tried hard, no doubt; there was no shirking to speak of,” he wrote. “But the game differed in no way that one could see from a hundred other games in which local rivalry has had no place whatsoever. The teams might have represented Penzance and Berwick-on-Tweed respectively for all the evidence the play gave to the contrary.”

In echoes of more modern times, the Guardian’s man also questioned whether modern players cared enough about the shirt on their backs.

“Is it reasonable to expect local or even club fervour in professional football as it exists today?” he wrote after United had won 2-1. “Can local patriotism thrive under a red jersey this year, a blue one the next, and perhaps a white one after that? It does not seem likely.”

Incredibly, Meredith kept playing until he was 49, helped, as the Guardian noted in his obituary, by being a details man whose “mind persistently dwelt on the problems of the game”.

Meredith, who was affectionately known as “old skin” and played with a toothpick in his mouth to help him concentrate, eventually called it a day four months before his 50th birthday when he took over a pub.

Not that it was a quiet retirement. During the Manchester blitz , for instance, a bomb exploded at the back of the pub and a shower of Welsh international caps scattered across the local neighbourhood. It took some time to collect them all given he played 51 times for his country.

Meredith was certainly a smart cookie too. When he was asked about the secret of City’s success, he openly admitted it was because the “club put aside the rule that no player should receive more than £4 a week”.

“Clubs are not punished for breaking the law – they are punished for being found out,” he also admitted. Which applies as much to 2026 as it did all more than a century ago.

items.lbText:
Net loss of £43m for year ended 30 June 2026

Revenue hits record £677.6m and forecast to grow

Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh ­successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019.

The financial results were released as it emerged United are raising revenue by selling small clumps of grass from the Old Trafford pitch to supporters. United relaid the playing surface for the first time in 14 years this summer , and an email to fans has offered them the chance to buy 7cm x 7cm clumps of turf for £125.

The £43m net loss for 2025-26 is a significant increase on the £33m for the previous 12 months, with compensation paid to the sacked manager Ruben Amorim a contributory factor along with the decision to increase the club’s borrowing facility by £93m to help fund the redevelopment of Old Trafford.

United’s continued losses come despite record revenue of £677.6m – up 1.7% on the previous 12 months – and the implementation of a major cost-cutting regime by Sir Jim Ratcliffe under which hundreds of staff have lost their jobs.

In discussing United’s results on an investor call, the chief executive, Omar Berrada, said the club’s summer transfer window, during which they spent £155m on three players, had been planned with “financial sustainability in mind” in an indication that the budget will continue to be tight for new manager, Michael Carrick.

That is underlined by the fact that United’s wage bill dropped to £301m, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100m lower than Manchester City’s.

While United reported operating profits of £22.6m for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 the increase in revenue was more than offset by the cost of financing the club. Net finance costs more than tripled to £69.2m from £21.2m in the previous year, partly owing to foreign-exchange ­movements, and the club refinanced several loans, increasing their net debt from £471.9m to £577.6m.

United sources have said the refinancing provided funding for the £63.5m purchase of a plot of land next to Old Trafford required to build their proposed new 100,000 capacity stadium, the first major investment in a complex project that could end up costing more than £2bn.

Berrada said the results demonstrated “the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football” and said: “This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.”

United are confident their financial outlook will improve over the next 12 months owing to the club’s return to the Champions League and the start of increased sponsorship deals with the training-kit partner Betway and shirt-sleeve partner SumUp, which will bring in £20m and £22m a year respectively. The club is forecasting revenue of between £740m and £760m for 2026-27.

items.title: Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking order
items.author: Paul MacInnes
items.content:
It is a symbol of the connection between the fanbase and club, but there is a growing fear executives would prefer stadiums full of one-off tourists

The document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
It is a symbol of the connection between the fanbase and club, but there is a growing fear executives would prefer stadiums full of one-off tourists

T he document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Nearly 150 years after fans started paying up front to watch their team, the season ticket remains a key component in the success of English football. It is also an enduring source of conflict between supporters and clubs, with tensions seemingly reaching new heights.

Arsenal, like United, have continued to act against the perceived misuse of tickets, suspending nearly 74,000 club accounts since they began a crackdown in 2024. This summer Chelsea became the latest club to insist on minimum levels of attendance to retain your ticket for the following season. Bournemouth moved 600 season-ticket holders to accommodate new hospitality seats and 14 out of the 20 top-flight sides raised their season-ticket prices.

Season-ticket holders have long felt undervalued. But there is a growing sense, especially among fans of the biggest clubs, that they are falling ever further down the pecking order as economic imperatives change. It is a feeling that intensified after a World Cup that seemed precision-tooled to extract as much money as possible from the most devoted fans. One Liverpool supporter crystallised common fears when he appeared on The Overlap at the start of the season arguing that a big club would soon try to get rid of season tickets altogether. The clip went viral.

The Football Supporters’ Association argues that clubs’ present behaviour shows an antagonism towards season-ticket holders. “There’s a sense from supporter groups at the most successful teams that their club executives and owners don’t fully appreciate season ticket holders and would rather have stadiums full of one-off visitors,” an FSA spokesperson said.

“Those who only measure things by the bottom line see season-ticket holders as a group whose matchday spend is lower than the once-a-year fan who will fill their bag at the club shop and pay a bigger premium for their ticket. It’s a shortsighted vision.”

The claim that clubs want to swap longstanding supporters for one-off tourists is at the heart of many fans’ fears over season tickets and, to a certain extent, it bears out. Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at the WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management in Düsseldorf, says season tickets “come at a cost” for clubs.

“In the Premier League , demand is way higher than seat supply,” Schreyer says. “But season-ticket holders get discounted seats, right? They are also more likely to be no-shows. When they do come they spend less on food, less on merchandise and they come later to the stadium. They also don’t churn, because these tickets are so scarce that nobody in their right mind would give them away. Every year the average age grows by one because there is no one new getting tickets. So for the clubs, there are a lot of economic problems from their season-ticket holders.”

That, however, is only one side of the ledger. “What we should not forget is that, in the end, season‑ticket holders are part of a product that, in the case of the Premier League, is marketed to a global audience,” Schreyer says.

“They are creating an atmosphere. Season-ticket holders are also used to all the rules and the rituals and the songs, the moments that make this experience very special. So tourists want to come because they want to experience it. If you were to get rid of all the season-ticket holders, you would have all the operational and coordination costs of doing it and the product would not be the same any more.”

There are other reasons why season tickets work for clubs, not least because they generate a largely predictable amount of revenue that turns up at the same time each year (at the very end of the season where it can be usefully deployed to help with transfer spending limits).

For most clubs, it would not be feasible to replace season‑ticket holders with one-off fans even if they wanted to. But with the average number of season tickets at any given Premier League fixture running at 75% of all tickets, is there a case that this number should not be set in stone? Could access to matches be broadened without killing off a part of what made them great?

“In theory, you could give all the seats to season-ticket holders and still have a lot of tickets for new fans if you manage it effectively,” Schreyer says. “You just need to change the mechanism in order to get the ticket that is unused on to the secondary market.”…

items.title: Keeping billionaires and the taxman happy | Letters
items.author: Guardian Staff
items.content:
says the super-rich could help guarantee a decent wage for low-paid people in return for some tax benefits. Plus letters from and

For this small compromise from the billionaires (who will still play the money markets and profit from others’ hard labour), the government could offer to reduce employers’ taxation costs by increasing the point at which low-paid people pay tax. Perhaps it could reduce national insurance payments for low-paid people, both employee and employer, thereby stopping the farce of the government paying income support to those on low incomes and then increasing taxation to fund it.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Stephen Gillian says the super-rich could help guarantee a decent wage for low-paid people in return for some tax benefits. Plus letters from Les Bright and Steve Brown

I have a simple solution to help keep the super-rich happy with their tax bills while keeping their enormous wealth safely stored offshore and allowing them possibly to spend more time in the UK ( Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit, 19 September ). They could insist that any company they earn their wealth from commits to paying all UK staff a decent living wage.

For this small compromise from the billionaires (who will still play the money markets and profit from others’ hard labour), the government could offer to reduce employers’ taxation costs by increasing the point at which low-paid people pay tax. Perhaps it could reduce national insurance payments for low-paid people, both employee and employer, thereby stopping the farce of the government paying income support to those on low incomes and then increasing taxation to fund it.

You might even argue that reducing taxation would steal the thunder from the shortsighted and status quo-enthused rightwing – possibly proving that the Labour party doesn’t have to tax to spend. What’s not to like? Stephen Gillian Shrewsbury, Shropshire

What is the BBC up to, giving its Big Boss interview slot to Jim Ratcliffe , a man who loves his country so much that he moved his affairs to Monaco six years ago to avoid paying his fair share of tax? He thinks that immigration and benefits are at the heart of our problems, but I’m inclined to think that his noxious views contribute to the division that is scarring the nation. Les Bright Exeter

Jim Ratcliffe has some gall, living as he does in a tax-free monarchical haven in the south of France. Does he ever connect with the ordinary people – some of whom still work at the football club he purports to support – who don’t have the luxury of being a multibillionaire paying less income tax than the working poor of Manchester do? Where is his sense of responsibility or awareness of the national interest? Words can hurt both individuals and nations, and for one so powerful, should be chosen with great care. Steve Brown Fontenay-sous-Bois, France

items.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Liverpool look stronger at the back, youngsters shine for Brighton and Brentford, and James Trafford makes his England case with Leeds

In the week that 16-year-old Max Dowman has been thrust into the spotlight, it was another teenager who gave us a glimpse of the future in Brighton’s impressive win over Arsenal. Charalampos Kostoulas – nicknamed ‘Babis’ in his homeland, in homage to former Argentina striker Gabriel Batistuta – has already started twice as many Premier League games as he did in his first season in English football, when he was a backup for Danny Welbeck. The 19-year-old repaid Fabian Hürzeler’s faith in him against the reigning champions. Despite his tender years, Kostoulas already possesses the physical attributes to mix it with the best. He caused Gabriel Magalhães and company problems all afternoon, capping it off with a brilliant goal from 25 yards, his third in eight days. “We always knew that he’s capable of scoring goals out of nowhere,” said Hürzeler. “He just has this intrinsic motivation of really improving every day. He gets more and more professional, he understands the demands from the Premier League more, he understands our demands.”

Continue reading...

items.lbText:
Michael Carrick insists team ‘kept pushing’ for leveller

Matheus Cunha: ‘Fulham put in more energy than us’

Michael Carrick rejected the suggestion that his Manchester United players lacked physical fitness after they snatched a last-gasp 1-1 draw at Fulham on Sunday. The statistics showed the home side ran a collective 6.6km more than United, whose goalscorer in the 89th minute – Matheus Cunha – was critical of his team’s efforts.

United were poor after the restart at 0-0, leading up to a disastrous Lisandro Martínez own goal in the 63rd minute, with Cunha saying they had to give more. “In the beginning of the second half, Fulham put in more energy than us and we cannot accept this,” Cunha said.

The draw was not the result Carrick or United wanted after a week during which they lost the derby against Manchester City and exited the Carabao Cup against Brighton; both matches were at Old Trafford. Carrick will take it under the circum­stances and he tried to ­highlight the positives which he said took in the never-say-die spirit of his ­players. They fought until the end and were rewarded when ­Cunha’s shot from distance took a heavy deflection off the ­Fulham defender David ­Affengruber to wrongfoot Bernd Leno.

Carrick said he did not agree with Cunha’s comment about the collective energy levels. “I don’t, ­particularly,” the manager said. “The way we finished the game … it didn’t look like that for me. I was quite happy with the way we finished the game. We kept pushing. I don’t think that’s an issue, no.

“The response [to the own goal] was really pleasing … the way we went about trying to get back into the game. [We] kept the ideas, kept the patience, kept the real purpose to it. We finished on a positive, which is a small step for us … without ­getting carried away it’s a good step. We came to take three points but at least we’ve taken something to build on ­moving forward.

“It has been pretty fine ­margins [so far this season] that have flipped it [the wrong way]. I know we can do better, we need to do better at certain things. But I’m not despondent and down because we’re showing some good signs.”

A section of the United support booed Carrick’s decision to ­withdraw Kobbie Mainoo in the 80th minute; the manager sent on Mason Mount in his place. “There’s always going to be ­certain reactions when you’re ­making changes,” Carrick said. “I ­understand. We’re chasing the game and ­everyone’s a little bit emotional. I don’t take any negatives or offence to it.”

Carrick was asked whether he felt a certain deflation among the fans, who have been expecting a big season from United. “It’s still a big season ahead,” he said. “It’s a long season and you’re going to have spells through it. That’s part of the journey.

“I’m not playing it down. We wanted more points. I’m not saying everything’s great. I understand the frustration. But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club. The players didn’t have that on the pitch today and that’s what will carry us through the season.”

The Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, was unhappy with the officials and he claimed they did not want United to lose after what had ­happened in the City game last ­Sunday when Erling Haaland’s ­winner was allowed to stand despite his teammate, Enzo Fernández, being in an offside position.

Arbeloa highlighted what he said was a soft free-kick in Harry ­Maguire’s favour on halfway, which came 35 seconds before Cunha’s equaliser. Maguire felt the contact from the ­Fulham substitute, César Palacios.

“All the fouls for them,” Arbeloa said to Sky Sports straight after the game. “You can see before they scored, the foul against Maguire … he’s a guy who is 100 kilos. Every decision was for them. And I knew. I knew after the game against Manchester City that they [would not] let Manchester United lose here.”

Arbeloa rowed back on his comments in his main press conference but still said he was “not really happy”. The referee, Peter Bankes, gave Fulham the benefit of the doubt in the 86th minute when a Martínez shot hit Calvin Bassey’s hand inside the area. Bassey did put his hand up but it remained close to his body.

items.title: Manchester United’s engine room runs out of steam as fans voice frustration | Jacob Steinberg
items.author: Jacob Steinberg at Craven Cottage
items.content:
Carrick’s side were short on inspiration, despite the summer spend in midfield, and the lack of quality in the final third was stark

One of the more damning aspects of Manchester United’s tortured rebuild is their inability to multitask. So much money has been frittered away, pushing United into the ridiculous position of going one position at a time each summer. Last year was all about the attack and the recent window was about central midfield, even though the options at full-back do not look strong enough to cope with a season back in the Champions League.

United remain a listless, drifting operation. The ownership is reviled and the fanbase is becoming increasingly mutinous. It was not just Gary Neville seeing red as he commentated on United’s dismal efforts away to winless Fulham. There was an ominous shift in the mood in the away end at Craven Cottage, summed up by the boos that greeted Michael Carrick substituting Kobbie Mainoo with 10 minutes to go.

items.lbText:
Carrick’s side were short on inspiration, despite the summer spend in midfield, and the lack of quality in the final third was stark

One of the more damning aspects of Manchester United’s tortured rebuild is their inability to multitask. So much money has been frittered away, pushing United into the ridiculous position of going one position at a time each summer. Last year was all about the attack and the recent window was about central midfield, even though the options at full-back do not look strong enough to cope with a season back in the Champions League.

United remain a listless, drifting operation. The ownership is reviled and the fanbase is becoming increasingly mutinous. It was not just Gary Neville seeing red as he commentated on United’s dismal efforts away to winless Fulham. There was an ominous shift in the mood in the away end at Craven Cottage, summed up by the boos that greeted Michael Carrick substituting Kobbie Mainoo with 10 minutes to go.

Carrick filled in as an emergency centre-back when United last lost this fixture, way back in December 2009. This has been a happy hunting ground since then and there was a sense of inevitability to United saving themselves on Sunday, although that was more to do with Fulham’s nerves at 1-0 up than any great show of defiance from the visitors when a third defeat in the space of a week was on the cards.

The late equaliser was fortunate , Matheus Cunha’s potshot hitting the luckless David Affengruber before going in. Bernd Leno was deceived in the Fulham goal but United did not fool anyone by stirring only after falling behind to Lisandro Martínez’s slapstick own goal. Speaking on Sky Sports, Neville called out the lack of effort during the 15 minutes before Fulham’s goal. Players went through the motions and pulled out of tackles, while the manner of the concession was feeble.

United could not get out of their box and when Cunha melted in a challenge with Calvin Bassey, the Fulham centre-back barrelled forward before testing Senne Lammens, only for Martínez to turn the rebound past his goalkeeper. It was a farcical goal and in keeping with the flow at that stage. United had no control or presence in midfield. Bruno Fernandes was the No 10 and Mainoo was deeper with Youri Tielemans, signed from Aston Villa last summer, but the ease with which Sander Berge and Shea Charles dominated for Fulham was proof that Carrick’s renovation in the engine room remains a work in progress.

It is interesting that United targeted quantity during a summer in which rival clubs were spending so much on midfielders. Andrey Santos, an unused substitute here, joined from Chelsea for £50m but is yet to prove himself in English football. Tielemans was an opportunistic £35m. Manchester City spent £300m on three midfielders, while Arsenal added depth by buying Bruno Guimarães for £75m. Carrick will hope that Carlos Baleba, back from an ankle injury, makes his debut after the international break.

United were outrun by Fulham. They looked unfit and need Baleba to provide oomph. There were times when Fulham ripped through the middle, particularly in transition. Alex Iwobi surged away from Tielemans during the first half. Josh King’s raids down the inside-right channel caught the eye and Fulham repeatedly cut through before half-time, only for poor finishing to let them down.

Carrick raised eyebrows by saying United controlled a lot of the first half. Cunha was close to the mark by saying Fulham “put in more energy than us” at the start of the second half. One worry is that the players are already not following Carrick’s instructions. Another is that the window-by-window rebuild has still left United short of ideas in midfield and attack.

Those areas were meant to have been sorted. Instead, United were ponderous on and off the ball. There were flashes in attack but they did not convince. While allowances have to be made for Benjamin Sesko missing out through injury, leaving United short of an effective target man to introduce, the lack of quality in the final third was stark.

Only a defensive error from Fulham led to Fernandes hitting the post at 0-0. Cunha also clipped the woodwork, albeit via a heavy deflection, and Marcus Rashford wasted two opportunities.

It is odd that the new-look attack still means a start for Rashford, who was up for sale last year. He played on the left and flattered to deceive before being taken off. Yet Rashford is not the only United forward who can look promising before drifting out of games. Bryan Mbeumo almost equalised but had an inconsistent game on the right. Cunha looks uncomfortable playing as the No 9 but Carrick does not appear to trust Sesko.

Carrick is under pressure. United have five points from five games and are already out of the Carabao Cup. The doubts over whether Carrick deserved the job will grow. But he is not the first United manager to struggle because of wider failings and is unlikely to be the last. It was not ideal, after all, that Carrick had to bring Joshua Zirkzee on when United were chasing an equaliser. The Dutch forward has five league goals since joining two years ago. Why has he not been sold? Some rebuild.

items.content:
To paraphrase a former Manchester United manager, Michael Carrick knew that the storm would come. Everything went a little too perfectly for him in the second half of last season. There would be ill winds at some point. Which was what Carrick could feel before this visit to Fulham. What were his emotions afterwards?

Relief was surely the main thing. Because after the derby defeat by Manchester City last Sunday and the midweek Carabao Cup exit against Brighton – both at Old Trafford – Carrick was starring at an unwanted hat-trick. All this on the back of other wobbles since the opening weekend when United lost at Hull. It is all extremely angsty and edgy.

items.lbText:
To paraphrase a former Manchester United manager, Michael Carrick knew that the storm would come. Everything went a little too perfectly for him in the second half of last season. There would be ill winds at some point. Which was what Carrick could feel before this visit to Fulham. What were his emotions afterwards?

Relief was surely the main thing. Because after the derby defeat by Manchester City last Sunday and the midweek Carabao Cup exit against Brighton – both at Old Trafford – Carrick was starring at an unwanted hat-trick. All this on the back of other wobbles since the opening weekend when United lost at Hull. It is all extremely angsty and edgy.

It was a darkly comic own goal by Lisandro Martínez that raised Fulham’s hopes of a first Premier League win under Álvaro Arbeloa; an episode in which the United goalkeeper, Senne Lammens, emerged with zero credit. Put it down as a colossal mess. United have almost always won in this corner of south‑west London in recent seasons. A crash against the team that started the day at the foot of the table was unthinkable.

Carrick and his side averted disaster when they caught a huge break with time almost up. There was little on for Matheus Cunha on the edge of the area, to the left of centre, and so he took on the shot for the near corner. The Fulham goalkeeper, Bernd Leno, looked to have it covered. Cue an almighty deflection off David Affengruber that sent the ball spinning into the opposite corner. United escaped.

It was true that Fulham invited pressure after the own goal. They sank back and came to lack an out‑ball. But it did not look as though United would find the required moment. Carrick’s players were too slow. Their moves were predictable. They could not get in behind in the second half, their only efforts coming from outside the area. Thankfully for Carrick, Cunha got one to work.

There was plenty to like about Fulham, who remain a work in progress under Arbeloa. He appears to have concluded that he needs greater security in central midfield – hence Sander Berge an d Shea Charles, with Alex Iwobi moved out to the left wing. There were round pegs in round holes for Fulham, which was not completely the case for United, albeit they were able to welcome back Luke Shaw on the left side of their defence.

With no Benjamin Sesko because of a recurrence of his shin issue, Carrick was without his only pure No 9. His solution, once again, was to use Cunha as a false 9 and ask Bruno Fernandes to play close to him. It was a box midfield, with Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo further back.

Arbeloa got his wingers, Oscar Bobb and Iwobi, to come inside to good effect. The battle for control of the middle of the pitch pulsed, with Josh King a major part of it.

The No 10 threatened during a first half in which Fulham were the more urgent and creative team. King worked Lammens in the 32nd minute after buying a yard of space from Shaw and it was not the only time that United felt their hearts skip.

Fulham had to be annoyed that they did not score before the interval. Twice, Gonzalo García fluffed his finish when well placed; on the second occasion, Berge extended Lammens on the second phase of the move. There was also the moment when Bobb spun into a seam of space only to drag wide. King wanted a free‑kick on the edge of the area in the 45th minute after running into Harry Maguire but he was looking for the contact and was booked correctly for diving.

United hit the woodwork twice in the first half and had other flickers. They got into some good positions only to lack composure. Cunha did well to wriggle clear of Affengruber on the right and pull back for Fernandes, who flicked against the far post. Cunha also saw his first deflected shot of the day loop high and drop down against the outside of the upright. Martínez forced Leno into a decent save early on. Marcus Rashford lifted a good chance high.

United lost their way after the restart. They lacked energy and could get nothing going. It was as if they hit a wall, and then came the gut punch of the own goal. It started when Cunha failed to hold up the ball in a deep midfield position. He was outmuscled by Calvin Bassey, who simply wanted it more. The Fulham captain pushed on to the edge of the area and when he unloaded, United’s problems were about to deepen.

Lammens’s parry was unconvincing and Martínez was ponderous. He could not set his feet properly and merely jabbed the ball towards his own goal – whereupon Lammens, perhaps wondering whether it was a back pass, tried to clear with his feet and got it all wrong.

United could feel the red panic lights flashing. They fought to stabilise and the plus point for Carrick was that his players kept going. Bryan Mbeumo and Cunha forced Leno into fine saves with curlers from distance. The key point was that they were from distance. Fulham looked poised to keep United at bay; they also went close to a second goal when Kevin, on as a substitute, forced Lammens into a save. Enter Cunha. He was the United saviour. The fault-lines for his team remain pronounced.

items.lbText:
Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire

Manchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.

In what was described as a “statement of no confidence” posted on X, MUMSC said: “Our players, staff, stewards, security teams and supporters come from different countries, cultures, ethnicities, religions and backgrounds. Manchester United would not be Manchester United without them.

“Manchester United does not belong emotionally to investment funds, shareholders or billionaires.

“After years of decline, broken promises and repeated failure, Manchester United Muslim Supporters’ Club has lost confidence in the current ownership structure of Manchester United Football Club.

“Enough is enough. It is time for change. The Glazers [co-owners] and Sir Jim Ratcliffe must go.”

Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giant Ineos , and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain was in decline because of high taxes and immigration.

His latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country was being “colonised by immigrants ”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.

MUMSC said it had challenged those remarks earlier this year, adding: “We hoped a lesson had been learned. Clearly, it has not.

“This week, Sir Jim has again placed immigration and people receiving benefits at the centre of his explanation for Britain’s problems, arguing that nobody is ‘tough enough’ to deal with either.

“We find these latest comments deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable.”

The billionaire told BBC News’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline.

He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk.

“But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”

Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.

He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.

“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident.

“And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.”

While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.

Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such as the 1958 .

The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.

Ratcliffe also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.

He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”

In response to the criticisms, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson told the BBC they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”

Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.

“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.

“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”

items.title: Heat is on Carrick but Wilcox must share blame for Manchester United’s woes
items.author: Will Unwin
items.content:
Recruitment is under scrutiny after £155m was spent on three midfielders while other positions were neglected

There was a mix of boos and apathy as Manchester United slumped out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday in their latest depressing act in domestic cup competitions. A solemn Michael Carrick and his players were the target for the jeers. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, looked unamused on his way out of the directors’ box but he and the hierarchy need to accept responsibility for their actions.

This is the natural course of football, where supporters know what is good or bad and give a rapid opinion to those whose wages they deem they pay. Carrick and his charges are the face of the club, the ones put up to speak with journalists and sent to promote the wares of sponsors.

items.lbText:
Recruitment is under scrutiny after £155m was spent on three midfielders while other positions were neglected

T here was a mix of boos and apathy as Manchester United slumped out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday in their latest depressing act in domestic cup competitions. A solemn Michael Carrick and his players were the target for the jeers. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, looked unamused on his way out of the directors’ box but he and the hierarchy need to accept responsibility for their actions.

This is the natural course of football, where supporters know what is good or bad and give a rapid opinion to those whose wages they deem they pay. Carrick and his charges are the face of the club, the ones put up to speak with journalists and sent to promote the wares of sponsors.

The head coach is often viewed as accountable for everything, from tactics to transfers, but the picture is more complex.

Carrick returned to United in January, but others have overseen the long-term strategy, within which the head coach sits. Pressure comes with his job, though, and a loss at Fulham on Sunday would significantly increase it.

United’s fanbase is fully aware of those running the club, with regular protests against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. They realise not everything happening over 90 minutes is the fault of the head coach and those wearing the shirt. The boos are for the one-off performance, the apathy for the bigger picture. It is tough for United supporters to see their club, back in the Champions League, outspent in the summer by promoted sides but this is the reality after years of financial mismanagement. It means the funds available have to be spent wisely.

United being two goals ahead against Brighton after 10 minutes and deservedly losing a game they were barely involved in for the remaining 80 is a strong indication things are not right within the team but Carrick knows this. Brighton were much changed but possess an exciting array of talent acquired from all over the world thanks to clever scouting and recruitment. They signed players from clubs in seven countries this summer, while United made four acquisitions from fellow Premier League clubs. Calculated risks and dynamism are part of the job but rarely seen at Old Trafford. It is somewhat ironic considering the most successful acquisition last summer was Senne Lammens from Royal Antwerp, in terms of price and consistency.

Carrick and Wilcox cannot truly be analysed until the most expensive of the three summer buys, Carlos Baleba, is available because his attributes should solve the lack of mobility. Targeting central midfielders was logical after the exit of Casemiro and inadequacy of Manuel Ugarte, but it was not the only area requiring attention. The overall deficiency of the squad was acknowledged internally but the lack of variety in strengthening felt naive and is proving to be so.

Buying players from other Premier League clubs is rarely cost-effective but there is a logic to limiting the adaptation time. Given the left-back shortage and Joshua Zirkzee’s inadequacies, sourcing a cheaper midfield option than the £50m Andrey Santos could have been advantageous for the wider health of the team. Someone needs to alleviate the pressure on Carrick by explaining why it was deemed best to spend £155m on three players in the same position. The outside world is left to pontificate, while Carrick creates a plan B when Luke Shaw, as many anticipated, has time out injured.

Wilcox has carried out internal media duties. On 30 October 2025, after three consecutive wins, he discussed the long-term plan, which was derailed by sacking Ruben Amorim just over two months later. Matters were going well when Wilcox opened up to United’s editorial staff but, apart from statements on sackings, he shows no appetite to speak amid downturns.

In Europe, sporting directors talking to the press is normal but the Premier League is yet to catch on, and the silence mounts at United with the team 13th.

Wilcox arrived, originally as technical director, from Southampton in 2024 and helped oversee the retention of Erik ten Hag after an eighth-placed finish. Ten Hag was belatedly dismissed for a poor start to the next season. Amorim was hired from Sporting despite his tactics not matching up with the squad available and a lack of finance to provide the overhaul required. United ended 15th and endured a meek Europa League final defeat by Tottenham. When Amorim was dismissed for his shortcomings after 14 months, Wilcox was permitted another chance to rectify the situation.

Carrick is not absolved of criticism; this United team are underperforming and pummelling promoted Ipswich and the Azerbaijan side Sabah cannot mask the disappointing start.

The defence has struggled, conceding seven goals in four Premier League games, and against Brighton the pairing of Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven was bordering on inept. The forward line has looked disjointed.

Wilcox was well respected when working as Manchester City’s head of academy, and those who dealt with him thought he was exceptional and suited to a role at that level. He is scrutinised and criticised for his work at United after moving up the chain. Many on the outside will be frustrated if JJ Gabriel departs but Wilcox would not be culpable, having worked hard to convince the player to stay, including via the teenager’s inner circle.

With power comes great responsibility at United but only Carrick is forced to embrace it. Ten Hag and Amorim have fallen for their failures, while others have been allowed to carry on. Carrick and Wilcox are equally invested in the success of the team but it seems only one will feel the consequences if things do not improve.

items.title: Premier League news: Carrick brushes aside questions over future, Arteta salutes ‘extraordinary’ Dowman

items.content:
United head coach believes it will take ‘a lot longer than one or two’ setbacks before he is concerned about his job

items.lbText:
United head coach believes it will take ‘a lot longer than one or two’ setbacks before he is concerned about his job

Premier League regulations do not allow players under 17 to be sent out on loan but Luton are understood to have registered an interest in Dowman, who was coached by their manager, Jack Wilshere, when he played for Arsenal’s under-18s. Arteta said it was possible Dowman could be allowed to leave in January, by which point he will be 17, but that his immediate future was at Arsenal.

“We haven’t really listened to any of the possibilities because we were crystal clear that we wanted to have him in the squad, that we wanted him to be part of the pre-season and then start to see where we are from there,” Arteta said.

“We will evaluate every six months, where we are and what is the best thing for him to do and then make the right decision. It depends on a lot of factors – what he needs and what the team needs as well, the availability we have in the squad, the minutes that he is playing and the qualities of those minutes. We have to be open but now the focus is to be here and to impact the team.” Ed Aarons

Roberto De Zerbi has insisted Sandro Tonali was not feeling the pressure of his price tag despite a mixed start to life at Tottenham. The midfielder became the most expensive player in the club’s history when he joined from Newcastle for £92.5m in the summer.

De Zerbi made a big play to sign Tonali amid interest from Manchester City and Arsenal, delivering a two-hour sales pitch to his fellow Italian to convince him to move to north London. He outlined how central Tonali would be to his plans and explained what he could expect from Spurs’ fans and the team’s style of football.

Tonali has started all four Premier League games this season – in which Spurs have drawn twice and lost twice without scoring – but has produced underwhelming defensive numbers and created only three chances.

De Zerbi revealed he had spoken to the 26-year-old about the weight of the price tag and claimed the player “doesn’t feel the pressure about that”. The Spurs manager pointed out that Tonali took time to adapt in his first season at Milan in 2020 before becoming one of the most sought-after young midfielders in the world once he settled there.

De Zerbi said “the adaptation has been not so fast” at Tottenham “but it can happen”, adding: “It is not so easy to change city, to change everything, for the players. Sometimes the adaptation is immediate, sometimes you need more time.”

Tottenham’s struggles in front of goal have not been helped by Tonali’s inability to create chances for the forwards. The goalless draw against Everton was the first in 140 games at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and followed a 0-0 at Nottingham Forest, thereby equalling Spurs’ tally of goalless games in the previous 181 matches. The last time they recorded three or more consecutive goalless draws in the league was 25 years ago under George Graham, when they went to four.

It is a remarkable run, especially after a summer spend of more than £300m, which leaves Spurs in 17th going into Saturday’s game against Aston Villa, who have also struggled after a summer of major change.

De Zerbi maintained he was happy with Tonali’s performances – even though he believed they could improve – and described him as “a complete midfielder”. “His physical characteristics are to play box-to-box but he started his career as a playmaker. He’s good enough with the ball, he’s good enough without the ball.” Sam Cunningham

Daniel Farke said Dominic Calvert-Lewin was “like a good wine” after the in-form striker’s call-up into Thomas Tuchel’s England squad . The 29-year-old has been included in the Three Lions’ squad for their Nations League matches after scoring four goals in six appearances in all competitions this season.

Calvert-Lewin was given a standing ovation by Leeds fans as he was withdrawn late on in Monday night’s 4-1 win against Newcastle at Elland Road. “Dominic is like a good wine, getting better by the year,” Farke said. “Physically, he’s on a top level and his pace is more than good enough I would say. He’s a very complete striker.”

He arrived at Leeds on a free transfer from Everton in August last year and when asked where he ranked among his best signings, Farke said: “At Leeds, while I’ve been here, we’ve made many top signings on a low budget.

“When I think about Joe Rodon, Ethan Ampadu, Ao Tanaka … It’s difficult to compare because as a striker you have a different role. But he’s definitely one of our better pieces of business. If you come as a free agent it doesn’t mean it costs no money because there’s a salary. But we believed in him when perhaps not many were doing this. He also believes in himself and he believes in Leeds United, so I would say he was a perfect fit.” Press Association

Barcelona and Bayern among other admirers

United hope they can convince 15-year-old to stay

Real Madrid are leading the race to sign the Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel after he told the Premier League club he wants to cancel his registration .

The 15-year-old has attracted interest from across Europe as his reputation has grown with academy performances. Barcelona have been keen to acquire him and Bayern Munich are known to admire the winger. It is understood Gabriel prefers a move to Europe and has an Irish EU passport through his father.

Although surprised by Gabriel’s decision, some at United felt he might not sign a professional contract as other clubs circled. United, however, still feel they may be able to rectify the matter having developed him since he joined at 11. He would be eligible to sign as a scholar when he turns 16 next month and as a professional a year later.

A move to Real Madrid comes with the prospect of accelerated progression to senior football with their B team, Castilla, who play in the regionalised Spanish third tier.

Had Gabriel not informed United of his desire to leave, he would have been called up by Michael Carrick for the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton on Wednesday. If he had played he would have become the youngest player in the club’s history.

“I just think we’ve got to be really careful of the whole situation,” Carrick said of Gabriel after the 3-2 defeat by Brighton.

“He’s a young boy. He’s 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players – their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure – we’ve got to be really conscious of that in this situation.”

Gabriel featured in a pre-season friendly against Atlético Madrid in Stockholm and has regularly trained with the first team recently.

‘I take responsibility … it doesn’t feel good at the moment’

United beaten 3-2 by Brighton after taking two-goal lead

Michael Carrick admitted Manchester United’s Carabao Cup capitulation against Brighton that was greeted by boos at Old Trafford was unacceptable and that answers had to be found at Fulham on Sunday.

United were knocked out 3-2 by Fabian Hürzeler’s visitors after leading 2-0 after 10 minutes through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount. Goals from Charalampos Kostoulas in first‑half added time, Pascal Gross on 65 minutes and Maxim De Cuyper four minutes later eliminated United.

It was the first time United had lost after leading 2-0 at Old Trafford for 50 years and the first time since 1984 they had been defeated there after being ahead at half-time.

Carrick’s side have beaten only Ipswich in the league and Sabah in the Champions League . “Under pressure? That doesn’t bother me one bit,” he said.

“I understand what goes on and how the world works. What bothers me is winning games and I believe we will do, but we have to do it pretty quickly. We can’t accept that [the manner of the defeat] as a group. I take responsibility for it. The performance towards the end of the second half, that’s on me. We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches. It doesn’t feel good at the moment.”

Carrick said of the boos at the end: “I totally understand the feelings of the supporters.”

The manager was asked about JJ Gabriel, the 15-year-old academy player who has informed United he wants to leave . “We have to be a little bit careful on that one. He’s a 15-year-old boy. It’s more about the welfare, the care and the attention of JJ as a child really,” Carrick said. “He’s certainly a young man. The situation is what it is, but we have to be careful about the exposure and how much we jump on that.”

Hürzeler, who made six changes, was delighted with the win. “I am not sure how many players on the pitch had experienced winning here, we have a lot of newcomers but when we play to our level we can compete with anyone in the league,” the Brighton manager said. In the next round his side will travel to the winner of the game on Thursday between Manchester City and Norwich. “We want to go as far as possible but if you want to win something you have to win at the highest level,” Hürzeler said.

items.title: De Cuyper and Brighton pile on pain for Manchester United with comeback
items.author: Jamie Jackson at Old Trafford
items.content:
Across four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby against Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabriel that he wants to leave, and now they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

items.lbText:
Across four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby against Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabriel that he wants to leave , and now they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

Capitulating after being 2-0 up may be the pick of these dizzying blows, as the prolonged boos at the final whistle suggested, and doing so ends a proud 50-year record: the last time the same lead at Old Trafford ended in defeat was Tottenham’s 3-2 win in September 1976.

When Marcus Rashford skated in with the chance to take the tie to 3-3 late on, there was no surprise he hit Jason Steele rather than the net.

Towards the end, Matheus Cunha was thrown on to join Bruno Fernandes, also a late substitute, illustrating how desperate Michael Carrick was. Yet Charalampos Kostoulas went close to scoring a second for Brighton, as United could not find a route to cancelling out Maxim De Cuyper’s 69th-minute strike that proved the winner.

After taking only four points from 12 in the league, serious questions will now be asked about where Carrick’s team are heading; they have to beat Fulham on Sunday to start correcting a dismal start to the season . The manager already looks haunted and he talked afterwards of not caring about being under pressure.

Carrick said the injustice suffered against City on Sunday would give his side an edge and Shea Lacey provided one when decorating a full debut with the sweetest of goals. The 19-year-old shimmied in Brighton’s area, beating Jaouen Hadjam before firing beyond a helpless Jason Steele. As impressive here was Benjamin Sesko’s hold-up work in the buildup as this allowed red shirts to flood forward, Youri Tielemans feeding Lacey.

This was eight minutes in and less than 120 seconds later Mason Mount doubled United’s advantage. Rashford’s pace and drive took him clear along the left, again inside the area. A trailing Steele boot saved the No 9’s effort but the ball bounced into Mount’s path and he drove home, via the turf, for a first goal since a win at Wolves last December .

Lacey’s strike drew a Carrick grin and delight from Mount, and you wondered how Gabriel – earmarked for the squad in this game, with the chance to become United’s youngest player – felt.

Brighton had lost only one of their previous five visits here and a flying start to the league campaign has Fabian Hürzeler’s team in fifth. Yet the 5-0 hammering of Coventry on Sunday already seemed distant as United continued to dominate.

Olivier Boscagli hit a corner straight out, summing up the visitors’ start, before Matt O’Riley forced Ayden Heaven into an error that led to another. This presaged a Seagulls renaissance that featured a lightning Malick Yalcouyé break but, clear in on the debutant Karl Darlow’s goal, the Ivorian spooned wide. The No 35 lacked the sharpness evident in a Rashford nutmeg of Chema Andrés which embarrassed the Brighton man and when Pascal Gross blasted over this was one more chance spurned by Hürzeler’s men.

But then came a goal – and real hope – for Brighton. Hadjam’s long left-right diagonal cut United’s rearguard clean out, and the slumbering Heaven allowed Kostoulas to scamper free, the striker beating Darlow through his legs.

Carrick, having beaten only Ipswich in the league and Sabah in Europe so far this season, needed a win, and as United (not under him) exited at the earliest opportunity in both domestic cups last season, progressing to at least a second tie in one of them would be welcome.

A wild Tielemans long-range shot that ballooned over failed to restore United’s two-goal lead but at least the home team were tapping the ball about, operating in Brighton territory, moving the visitors around.

A Sesko burst from halfway had the onrushing Steele hacking away just in time. United were in control. But the question was: could they maintain this and register the type of mature, accomplished display that would show an evolution in Carrick’s team? Sesko, in yards of space, dawdling and being dispossessed when a simple ball would have fed Lacey, suggested not.

A loose Rashford pass aimed for Sesko hinted at the same. More promising was a pass for Noussair Mazraoui as he drove into the area along the left channel, as was the subsequent corner that created an opening Tielemans narrowly missed.

But then calamity. Diogo Dalot’s hoofed clearance failed to find Sesko as Luka Vuskovic headed to Gross; Brighton’s captain made room and netted with ease. Even worse followed. Brighton raided along the right, Kostoulas’s cross pinged off Mazraoui’s backside, and there was De Cuyper to finish.

On 72 minutes Carrick played his ace, introducing Fernandes for Mount, then followed up with Cunha. But United remained toothless.

items.lbText:
15-year-old wants his registration to be cancelled

He was to be in squad to face Brighton on Wednesday

Manchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.

Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.

United are unsure what has prompted this decision and believe they have done everything they can to show Gabriel and his family there is a pathway to the first team. Those efforts have included meetings with Ruben Amorim, when the Portuguese was head coach, and Sir Alex Ferguson.

United believe the situation, first reported by the Telegraph , is rectifiable given the time remaining on Gabriel’s contract. Club officials say the player has a deal to the end of the season and cannot be deregistered despite his request. The north London-born Gabriel cannot sign a professional contract until he turns 17 in October next year, but can sign a scholarship agreement when he turns 16.

Gabriel, who has been with United since the age of 11, has emerged as one of the most exciting prospects at Carrington in years, scoring a hatful of goals for the youth teams, most recently a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut against Sabah last week. He regularly plays for older age groups at United, scoring 26 goals in 29 games last season, and has made two appearances for England Under-17s. Gabriel is also the most recent, and youngest, winner of United’s prestigious Jimmy Murphy young player of the year award. He has regularly trained with the first team.

Speaking after that 5-0 win against Sabah, Adam Lawrence, United’s lead under-21 coach, said: “JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through. He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.

“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into.”

Barcelona and Manchester City have been linked previously with Gabriel, after reports emerged last year suggesting the player’s family would be planning to move him.
